WASHINGTON, Oct 28 : The United States on Wednesday banned imports from three Chinese genomics companies for allegedly working with the government of Xinjiang to enable the forced labor of Uyghur and other ethnic minorities. The companies are BGI Genomics Co.. Ltd, (300676.SZ), MGI Tech Co Ltd. (688114.SS) and Shenzhen BGI Technology Co Ltd, which the U.S. says is also known as the BGI Group. The companies were added to the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act Entity List, according to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which identifies entities that use or facilitate the use of forced labor of Uyghurs and other minorities, or source material from the Xinjiang region. Beijing has regularly dismissed accusations of forced labor and other abuses against Uyghurs and other Muslim minorities in the Xinjiang region

Source: Reuters

Oct 28 : Telenor's efforts to persuade mobile customers to pay more for network quality and security services could face a new test from AI shopping agents expected to focus heavily on price, executives said on Wednesday. The Norwegian operator's "more-for-more" strategy adds benefits to subscriptions to encourage higher spending. Its task is to make those extras count when customers compare offers. AI agents would be "to a large degree price driven", CEO Benedicte Schilbred Fasmer told Reuters, saying the benefits beyond connectivity needed to be clear to customers. That would add another dimension to an already competitive market. Telenor lost 22,000 mobile subscriptions in Norway in the third quarter, while mobile revenue per user rose 2.7 per cent year on year.

CFO Torbjorn Wist argued in a call with analysts that prices were already transparent and that coverage, capacity and security would remain a "strategic moat". He also saw agents as a possible route to customers, provided Telenor could exchange information with them. The concern extends beyond telecoms. Payments firm Adyen told Reuters in August that merchants feared losing direct customer relationships and repeat business as shoppers increasingly turned to AI chatbots. Fasmer said Nordic identification requirements would keep people involved in subscription changes. Asked about competition in Norway, she remained confident in the existing strategy, although its pace could slow in some markets. "But we don't think we've run out of road on the more-for-more strategy," she said. Telenor is building a more Nordic-focused business, adding services such as security alongside connectivity while reducing its exposure in riskier Asian markets.

Source: Reuters

Oct 28 : Puerto Rico's seven-division world champion Amanda Serrano will retire after defending her unified featherweight world titles against Australia's Skye Falzon on home soil, in a fight her promoter dubbed "The Last Walk". Most Valuable Promotions said Serrano, who holds a 50–4–1 record with 32 knockouts, will defend her unified WBO and WBA featherweight world titles on January 9 at Coliseo de Puerto Rico in San Juan. Puerto Rico's only undisputed boxing champion is also gunning for the all-time women's knockout record which the 38-year-old jointly shares with American Christy Martin. "Boxing has been my life and I never could have imagined the journey it would take me and my family on," Serrano said in a statement.

"From the early days when women's boxing was fighting for recognition in small theatre shows, to headlining Madison Square Garden in New York, reaching millions of fans around the world on the biggest shows, and helping open doors for the next generation of female fighters... I always believed and I'm proud of everything we've accomplished." Serrano made history alongside Ireland's Katie Taylor in 2022 when they became the first women boxers to headline New York's Madison Square Garden. The highest-profile rivalry in women's boxing produced a trilogy of fights which Taylor swept via a majority decision in 2025. A Guinness World Record holder for winning titles across seven weight divisions, Serrano also became a leading voice for equality in women's boxing. In 2023, she competed in the first women's unified world championship bout over 12 three-minute rounds, later voluntarily vacating her WBC title rather than abandon her commitment to equal rules. "'The Last Walk' is a celebration of an athlete who changed the sport forever... We're proud to give Amanda the farewell she deserves," said Nakisa Bidarian and Jake Paul, founders of Most Valuable Promotions. "Saturday, January 9, will mark the end of an extraordinary career inside the ring, but Amanda's legacy will live on through every female fighter who follows in her footsteps." Falzon, who is also 38, holds a 12-2 record with seven knockouts.

Source: Reuters

Oct 28 : Cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase is adding Ripple's stablecoin RLUSD to its platform, expanding its slate of dollar-backed crypto tokens.  The move is a boost for blockchain payments company Ripple, which launched RLUSD in December 2024 to facilitate near-instant settlement of cross-border payments. The stablecoin has a market capitalization of more than $2.5 billion, according to data provider CoinGecko.  RLUSD will be available starting Wednesday across Coinbase's retail and institutional platforms, Coinbase said. For years, Circle's USDC was the flagship stablecoin Coinbase offered to its customers, but Coinbase has gradually expanded its stablecoin offerings to include PayPal's PYUSD, as well as Open USD, a stablecoin issued through a joint venture backed by Visa, Mastercard and Coinbase.   "It's a really credentializing moment for RLUSD to not only be listed on Coinbase but to be embraced across the platform," said Jack McDonald, senior vice president of stablecoins at Ripple.  Stablecoins are digital tokens designed to keep a constant value and backed by traditional currencies, most commonly the US dollar. They are used mainly to trade in and out of other cryptocurrencies, such as bitcoin, but proponents say they can also facilitate instant payments and corporate treasury management.

Source: Reuters

BERLIN, Oct 28 : Winning the Ballon d'Or will help convince Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane to extend his deal with the German champions, former World Cup winner Lothar Matthaeus said on Wednesday. On Monday Kane became the first Englishman to win the prestigious award - the top individual honour in the sport - since Michael Owen in 2001. The England captain was prolific last season, scoring 61 goals in 51 games for Bayern across all competitions as the German side completed a domestic league and cup double. He was also a World Cup semi-finalist with England, scoring six goals in the tournament. "We are very happy to have Harry Kane in the Bundesliga. He is an international ambassador of football," Matthaeus, who won the award in 1990 after leading Germany to World Cup victory that year, said in an online media round table.

Kane, 33, joined Bayern in 2023 in a €100 million ($111 million) move from boyhood club Tottenham Hotspur, in search of silverware. He has since won the league twice and is in talks with Bayern over a new contract. "I think he gets a bonus (for winning the Ballon d'Or), 36 years ago I got nothing," Matthaeus said. "But it is about more than money. It is a good moment to sign (a new deal) for Bayern. Bayern helped him get this Ballon d'Or. "The relationship between Harry Kane and Bayern Munich is perfect, and with everything that has happened in the last three years, I think Harry will sign his contract for the next two, three years." Oct 28 : Former Japan coach Takeshi Okada has resigned as vice-president of the Japan Football Association, citing concerns over developments surrounding FIFA and the World Cup, the JFA said on Wednesday. Okada's resignation came a week after Asian Football Confederation (AFC) president Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa declared support for Gianni Infantino's bid for re-election as FIFA president at the AFC's extraordinary congress in Tokyo. The endorsement marked a sharp shift from the AFC's position three months earlier, when the confederation accused FIFA of a "fundamental breach of trust" over the abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal to sell a stake in FIFA competitions. "Guided by my belief that sports should embody integrity, I have always valued their social significance," Okada said in a statement on the JFA website.

As a sportsman, I cannot accept this, which has led me to make this decision." Infantino, who has led FIFA since 2016, is seeking re-election in March after apologising for his failed private investment project. Support from Asia, one of FIFA's largest voting blocs, could prove crucial to his bid. "Given the relationship with the Asian Football Confederation and the impact on Japanese soccer, I understand that there are practical reasons for aligning with the AFC's stance," Okada said. Okada coached Japan at the 1998 and 2010 World Cups, leading the team to the last 16 in South Africa.

Source: Reuters

BEIJING: Liu Yandong, China's former vice premier and a former member of the elite Politburo, died in Beijing on Wednesday, state-run Xinhua news agency said. Liu, who was 80 when she died,was widely regarded as the most prominent and highest-ranking female official in China during much of her tenure in the country's male-dominated political leadership. LOS ANGELES, Oct 28 : Apple is expected to unveil its first touchscreen MacBooks on Wednesday, abandoning a long-held aversion to the technology as it caps a burst of product launches ahead of the crucial holiday shopping season. Apple is holding an event in Los Angeles after launching a folding iPhone, Duo, at its Silicon Valley headquarters in September and a smart home hub in New York earlier this month. While those products will test new markets for Apple, the Los Angeles event could rekindle an old question: should Apple put the touchscreens that it made mainstream in iPhones and iPads in its oldest product line? Apple executives long resisted the idea, with Steve Jobs saying in 2010 that touchscreens on laptops were "ergonomically terrible" and then-CEO Tim Cook saying in 2012 that such devices would be as pleasing to users as converging a toaster and a refrigerator. Before becoming Apple's current CEO, John Ternus argued that Apple already made a touchscreen computer with its iPad lineup. But touchscreens have been widely available for more than a decade on Windows devices, and with the iPhone nearing its two-decade anniversary, a new generation of buyers expects screens to respond to touch.

"I believe they were always wrong on pushing back on touch, and this is the long arm of reality setting in," said Anshel Sag, an analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy. "Some things are purely inevitable." A key question for Apple is how customers will respond. The company has seen an uptick in Mac sales, but much of that growth has been among technology enthusiasts and businesses buying the machines to handle AI tasks on-device. While Apple this week announced an upgraded base model of its MacBook Pro with a new M6 chip, Bloomberg News has reported that it plans to ship touchscreen models with its existing M5 Pro and M5 Max chips that already come in MacBook Pro models, meaning the new machines would not gain a significant performance boost over existing ones. "The only thing people want is more memory and better processors for local models!" prominent tech commentator Jason Calacanis, the host of the All-In Podcast, wrote on X.

FAST

LONDON/HONG KONG, Oct 28 : With jet fuel prices at roughly double their levels before the Iran war, airlines are growing increasingly reluctant to lock in future fuel costs through new hedges, warning instead of steep fare increases to offset higher fuel bills. Hedging allows airlines to lock in future fuel prices, helping shield them from increases and providing greater certainty over costs. But some programmes require premiums, collateral or other costs, while airlines that hedge at current elevated prices risk being locked into expensive fuel if geopolitical tensions ease and prices retreat. As the conflict in the Middle East enters its ninth month, the strategy shift means fliers globally will likely pay far higher air fares as carriers lose their hedging protection, testing consumer willingness to shell out more for travel. "Most hedging is finishing," AirAsia CEO Tony Fernandes told Reuters this month, adding the Malaysian airline was budgeting for 12 months of high oil prices and had "given up trying to predict" how geopolitical tensions would evolve.

He said the firm was not even modelling a scenario where oil prices fall. "So everyone's going to be exposed. There's only one way or two ways of dealing with that: cut costs or raise fares." Finland's Finnair, which said this month that high fuel costs had fed through to ticket prices, has stopped adding new hedges as fuel costs surged this year. It has an average hedging ratio of 34 per cent for 2027. "With such high prices, how do you then lock in low prices again?" finance chief Pia Aaltonen-Forsell said on Tuesday. "If we add right now, it's more expensive." NO EUROPEAN AIRLINE WELL HEDGED THROUGH 2027, RYANAIR SAYS Jet fuel accounts for between 30 per cent and 40 per cent of airlines' costs, with European and Asian carriers historically hedging more of their fuel needs than US rivals, which largely abandoned the practice after costly bets on oil prices backfired. "You have stability of cost when you hedge," said Jeffrey Goh, managing director at Alton Aviation, adding it remained a bet on prices rising — and could backfire. "You have to look at the forward curve and predict how fast it might go down." The pressure could intensify in 2027 as hedges put in place before the war expire, exposing airlines more fully to current fuel prices. "None of the European airlines, including Ryanair, are well-hedged until summer of 2027, so I think you're going to have to see air fares rise by 15 per cent to 20 per cent," Ryanair CEO Michael O'Leary told reporters earlier this month. Ryanair said in September it had stopped hedging. Europe's largest airline has hedged about 80 per cent of its jet fuel needs for the year ending March 2027. In a sign of challenges airlines may face pushing higher fares, budget carrier Norwegian Air Shuttle said on Wednesday it had been forced to undo some post-Iran war price hikes because customers "were not willing to pay". FUEL HEDGING NOT A 'COMPLETE SOLUTION' Globally, airline hedging policies remain fragmented, with some carriers expanding programmes since the war began and others dialling them back. Carriers with weak balance sheets also often have less flexibility to absorb the costs associated with hedging and can be fully exposed to fuel-price movements, contributing to a flurry of recent bankruptcy and insolvency filings. US airlines have largely shown little appetite to return to hedging despite this year's fuel shock. Analysts say US consumers tend to be less price sensitive than travellers in other regions and the most willing to absorb higher fares. Air fares in the European Union rose 5.8 per cent year-on-year in September, the latest official data show. US air fares, meanwhile, were up more than 20 per cent year-on-year in the month. American, United, Delta, JetBlue and Allegiant have no material fuel hedges, while Frontier has no active hedging position. Southwest ended its long-running programme last year, while Alaska and Hawaiian also closed out remaining positions. The reluctance of some European and Asian airlines to add new hedges could signal a broader shift in industry attitudes towards fuel hedging, although this year's fuel-price spike has also highlighted the risks of remaining exposed to fuel markets. Delta, United and Southwest all cut profit targets or disappointed investors with their earnings outlooks this month as fuel expenses climbed. Despite hedging more than 70 per cent of their jet fuel needs for this year, Ryanair and Lufthansa cut capacity on some routes to limit the impact of unhedged fuel costs. "Fuel remains the single largest area of uncertainty in the outlook," said Air New Zealand Chief Financial Officer Kris Cudmore. "Our hedging program provides some nearer term protection, but it is far from a complete solution."

(Additional reporting by Phil Blenkinsop in Brussels, Rajesh Kumar Singh in Chicago and Julie Zhu in Hong Kong and Essi Lehto in Helsinki; Editing by Adam Jourdan and Mark Potter)

Source: Reuters

SEOUL, Oct 28 : South Korea's Media and Communications Commission has fined Google and Apple for limiting users to specific app payment systems and ordered corrective measures, the regulator said on Wednesday. Google was fined 42.9 billion won ($32.35 million) and Apple 20.8 billion won, the commission said in a statement. Apple said it disagreed with the decision and was evaluating options in accordance with South Korean laws. It said it has worked with outside developers to enable innovation through its App Store.
